Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").

- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why1: Right after I said nobody else has to agree, it makes sense to show me the list Keel will test and let me check it.
screens.why2: The rows are in my own words: 'deaf and hard-of-hearing adult', 'has the problem', 'decides to buy', 'nobody else'. The title just repeats in the intro, which is clumsy but not confusing.
screens.why3: Who decides on a $599 pair of glasses is something I know from my own customers: the wearer buys them, often with HSA/FSA money.
screens.why4: The same person shows up twice, once as 'has the problem' and once as 'decides to buy', so two rows overlap where one would do; 'Nobody else' carries no tag.
screens.why5: It still means what I said: the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree.
screens.why7: Nobody else comes first and no role was invented, so the belief 'nobody else' matches what I said. But the card says the person with the problem and the decider share one row when they are the same person, and that every row carries a tag; here the wearer is split into two rows and 'Nobody else' has no tag.
screens.instead: The people involved: Nobody else · does not have to agree; Deaf or hard-of-hearing adult · has the problem and decides to buy -- confirm, or add up to two who have to agree.

screens.why1: Right after I said nobody else has to agree, this confirms that answer before Keel tests it, so it is obvious why it is here.
screens.why2: The title and belief are plain, but the bar's 'the last time they paid for something for this' is clumsy and takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know my wearers buy these themselves, HSA/FSA and all, so confirming that the wearer decides alone is squarely my life.
screens.why4: A list holding only Nobody else becomes a statement to confirm, with continue or go back as the only choices; nothing is missing or odd for a single fixed row.
screens.why5: It keeps exactly what I picked: the wearer decides and nobody else has to agree, with no role added that I never named.
screens.why7: The card says a list holding only Nobody else is a statement to confirm, the belief reads 'nobody else must agree first' to match my list, and the bar counts only decided alone as support, as the card requires.
screens.instead: Keel will test: The deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides alone; holds if at least 2 in 3 say they decided on their own the last time they paid for something to help them follow conversations.

screens.why1: After who pays and the price, asking what first step I'd want a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult to take is the obvious next question in 'will they pay'.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint's examples ('pay for a pilot', 'let us run a trial') and 'where any money goes' come from B2B selling, not from selling glasses to one person, so I had to translate them before typing 'order the caption glasses with free returns'.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I want a buyer to do first, because we offer 15-day risk-free returns on the glasses.
screens.why4: The only chip is 'I'm not sure', which the card allows for the founder, and it fits a box where I type my own step.
screens.why5: My step, 'order the caption glasses with free returns', is kept whole, including the product and the free returns that define it.
screens.why7: The box asks for one step in base form, at most 9 words, naming what it costs, with 'I'm not sure' allowed and a smaller free step promised on the next screen, all as the card requires; my answer fits that shape.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want them to take? e.g. "order a pair with free returns" or "try them at a demo" (up to 9 words; if it costs money, Keel suggests a free step next).

screens.why1: After I typed my first step, it makes sense to show it back with the four answers strangers will get and the belief Keel will test.
screens.why2: The step and the four answers read cleanly, but the smaller-step field shows 'Yes, after try a pair of caption glasses first', which is ungrammatical and has the answer frame stuck to the front, so I had to read it twice to see what Keel actually saved.
screens.why3: Whether to order a pair of caption glasses on a free-return window is a decision my wearers make themselves with their own money, often HSA/FSA, so they can answer it from their own lives.
screens.why4: The four answers are complete and in the right order, but the soft yes 'after trying a pair first' nearly overlaps with the step, because the only way to try AirCaps is to order a pair and send it back within 15 days.
screens.why5: 'Order the caption glasses with free returns' keeps my words, including the free-returns term that defines the step, and the belief says exactly what I meant.
screens.why7: The rules are mostly met (the step leads the list, a soft yes and two against, no escape, a belief that can hold or fail), but the smaller step is drafted as a broken answer fragment instead of a noun phrase, and 'trying a pair' is not a no-cost step separate from ordering with free returns for a product that has no try-on outside the order.
screens.instead: Smaller step: 'a free caption demo on my phone'. Answers: Yes, I'd order the caption glasses with free returns · Probably, after a free caption demo on my phone first · Probably not · No

screens.why1: Right after I set the first real step (order the caption glasses with free returns), asking whether to invite respondents to try it is the obvious next move before the study goes out.
screens.why2: Short and plain; the hint says exactly what respondents will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want a list of people ready to try AirCaps is entirely my own call as the founder.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it; the two are distinct and need no escape.
screens.why5: The hint's line 'Would you try this for real? Leave your email.' doesn't echo my typed step 'order the caption glasses with free returns', so I can't tell from this screen whether respondents will see my actual commitment or a generic try-it line.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you order the caption glasses with free returns? Leave your email." — Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Picking who runs the interviews is the natural last setup step before the link goes out, right after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: Two named voices with a 5-second sample, plus a clear credit cost and how the link is sent, is plain to me on first read.
screens.why3: I can judge which voice and face I want speaking for my study, though Keel only lets me hear the samples, not see whether the face is easy to lipread.
screens.why4: For my respondents the real choice is a text-first or captioned interview with a face that is easy to lipread, and neither option is that; a voice pick alone barely matters to most deaf people.
screens.why5: Nothing of AirCaps or the roles leaks; the screen only names my respondents as I typed them, deaf or hard-of-hearing adults.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults get your questions? — Written on screen with captions (no voice needed) / Daphne on video, captioned and easy to lipread / Saskia on video, captioned and easy to lipread

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers will answer belongs right after choosing who asks and just before sending, so it is obvious why it comes here.
screens.why2: AI interviewer, read and tap, and let them choose are each explained in a plain line, and I can pick at once.
screens.why3: I know my people: many of them lean on text, and some don't use their voice much, so I can judge which format they would get through.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and complete for a general audience, but for deaf adults 'asks each question aloud on video' leads with the one channel they can't rely on, and Deaf ASL signers like the instructor in my own stories have no signed option.
screens.why5: The screen names my respondents as I typed them, deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, and nothing of AirCaps or the glasses leaks into how they answer.
screens.instead: How should deaf and hard-of-hearing adults answer? -- Read and tap (questions written, answers tapped or typed) / AI interviewer Daphne (on video with every question captioned, answer by typing, tapping or talking) / Let them choose

screens.why1: Once the interviews are set up, choosing who gets a link is the obvious last step before sending, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: Plain words throughout; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own screen, which I have just been using, and 'open link' and 'signs in with Google' are clear to me.
screens.why3: I know whether I am reaching deaf and hard-of-hearing people I know by name (early users, the waitlist, friends from the TranscribeGlass days) or posting into a community group, so I can answer from my own situation.
screens.why4: The three routes (named people, a Keel search list, one open link posted where the community already is) are distinct and cover how I would reach people, and a choice of channel needs no escape chip.
screens.why5: Nothing here rewrites my idea or roles, and nothing about AirCaps leaks to the people who will be interviewed.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right under the title with its deciding number, 1 of 7 against a bar of 5, and the line 'the verdict is the worst of all its cards' explains why that card sets it.
screens.why_b2: Each card's count and bar are plain, but the cards skip from 4 to 6 with no 5, and the Price line 'bar 5 of 7 on each' over two prices takes a second look.
screens.why_b3: Price is recognisable as $599 up front then an optional $20 a month rather than the $599 to $839 a year I framed, and Existing sacrifice is now counted in lost conversations rather than the dollar estimate I typed, so both are reworded but still mine.
screens.why_b4: The card lines ('they value it below your price', 'they lose less today than you estimated') say what failed but not what to do: whether to drop the price, lead on HSA/FSA, or retarget the segment.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible on every card and nothing is called strong, but the screen never says 7 is a small count and states 'they lose less today than you estimated' as fact about all deaf and hard-of-hearing adults.
screens.instead: Not holding up: none of 7 would pay $599 and only 1 of 7 loses 12+ conversations a month. Only 7 answered, so test a lower entry price or a narrower, group-heavy segment before reading this as final.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside the count that decides it: 1 of 7 at 12 or more against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b2: The cells, the 7 counted and the bar at 5 of 7 are plain, but the axis unit 'conversations of the conversations they are in a month' pushes my count through a share frame, so I had to read it twice.
screens.why_b3: Existing sacrifice and 'about 12 conversations a month: conversations they lost the thread of' are my numbers and my loss line, though the 'per person' from the stage page is dropped here.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the count and points to the Price card, but it does not tell me what this means for selling AirCaps, such as not pitching on a cost my wearers do not feel at 12 a month.
screens.why_b5: The card flags 'a small group: a lean, not a call', but the headline 'they lose less today than you estimated' speaks for everyone off answers to 'fell through', which is a different and rarer thing than losing the thread.
screens.instead: Ask 'Last month, about how many conversations did you lose the thread of?', label the strip 'conversations per person a month', and say: 'Among these 7, most lost fewer than 12 (median 8); a lean, not a call, so do not lead the pitch on how many conversations they lose.'

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside the deciding numbers: 0 of 7 at $599 or more up front and 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month, against a bar of 5 of 7 on each.
screens.why_b2: Both ladders show plainly what is counted (the up-front band, then the monthly band), over 7 people, with my $599 and $20 marked as band low edges and the bar at 5 of 7 under each.
screens.why_b3: It names AirCaps, my $599 for the glasses and the optional $20 a month Pro plan, which is how I actually charge, and the deaf and hard-of-hearing adults I am selling to.
screens.why_b4: The So line gives the band most people chose ($250 to under $599, 6 of 7) and then sends me to the Insights tab, but it does not say what this means for my price, such as a lower entry price or a try-before-you-buy pair, which several of the quotes point straight at.
screens.why_b5: With 0 of 7 the verdict is not overstated, n stays visible, and the count line says outright that a small group is a lean, not a call.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 put AirCaps at $250 to under $599, just under your $599, and several want to try a pair before ordering; with 7 people this is a lean, so test a lower up-front price or a borrow-first trial, and remember the $20 plan is optional, so the up-front price is the one to settle first.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Not reached' sits right beside its deciding number, '0 of 7 named your price or more', and the count line and the list of people both back it up.
screens.why_b2: Three bars all at 0 make clear nobody was counted, but the strip shows 5 ghost cells against the 7 people who answered and no 2-in-3 bar marker is drawn, so I have to stop and work out what the 5 means.
screens.why_b3: The $599 up front and optional $20 a month are my numbers, but 'could find it in money they already spend on this' is Keel's derived budget belief, shown as 'your belief' when I never typed or checked it.
screens.why_b4: The So line says the card waits until 5 people reach my price, which points back at Price, but it doesn't say the real move: price drew everyone to $250 to under $599 up front and under $20 a month, so retest at that or reshape the offer.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing about where the money would come from, says nobody was asked because all 7 named less, and keeps n visible; 'Only 0 of 7' is clumsy but not an overstatement.
screens.instead: Not reached: all 7 priced it below $599 (6 at $250 to under $599, 1 under $250), so nobody was asked where the money would come from; Keel's derived belief that they'd pay from money already spent stays untested until a lower price, say under $599 up front, is retested on Price.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, '6 of 7 decided alone · bar 5 of 7', so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts who had to agree, across seven people, with each option marked for or against, and the strip puts my bar plainly at 5 of 7 with six for and one against.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer is the dimension I checked, and the line saying the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides with nobody else agreeing is the 'Nobody else' I picked, in my study's own words.
screens.why_b4: The So line only repeats the count ('They decide alone... 1 of 7 needed someone's agreement') and never tells me what follows, for example that I can sell straight to the wearer and that the barrier is price, not sign-off.
screens.why_b5: n is visible throughout (7 answered, 7 counted), and the screen itself says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so it doesn't oversell six of seven.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 paid for something like this on their own, so sell straight to the wearer with no one else to convince; the obstacle on this stage is the price, not who signs off.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 said yes and bar 5 of 7, so I know the belief held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against and the marker at 5, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Commitment and 'order the caption glasses with free returns' are my step as I last checked it, though the rule line's 'probably, after try a pair' is a grammar slip in a row nobody picked.
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' doesn't say what to book them into, and for a $599 purchase it doesn't tell me what to do with six people who say they'd order.
screens.why_b5: The count line rightly calls 7 a lean, but the So line then acts on it as settled, with no word that the question carried no price while the Price card showed 0 of 7 valued it at $599.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 would order with free returns, a lean from 7 that was asked without the price; send the six an order page at $599 and count who actually orders.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside its deciding numbers: 0 of 7 at $599 up front and 0 of 7 at $20 a month, against a bar of 5 of 7 on each.
screens.why_b3: The line is named Price and the belief reads my own $599 up front and optional $20 a month, as I typed it.
screens.why_b4: The screen itself never says what the failure means for the idea. The quotes point at a concrete move (a demo or borrowed pair before ordering), but I have to draw that out myself, and the grouping was still loading.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible throughout: 7 against, 6 asked here, Amaka named as never seeing it, and each quote carries its own price bands, so nothing claims more than the six who answered.
screens.why_b6: It tells me things I did not type: people want to try a pair in their own hard setting (stage lights, a noisy walk) even though I already offer 15-day returns, crosstalk and audience questions are where worth gets proven, and most put the glasses at $250 to $599 and the plan under $10.
screens.instead: Say it outright: nobody reached $599. Most would pay $250 to $599 up front and under $10 a month, and they want to try it in their own hard setting first, so lead with the 15-day returns as a try-at-home offer and test a lower price.

screens.why1: As the opening screen it makes sense to check first that I actually talk with hearing people regularly, since that is what the whole study is about.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is how I and other deaf people say it every day, and the sentence is short enough to take in at one look or one hearing.
screens.why3: I know without guessing that I deal with hearing people every week, at the shop, at work and with family.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it with nothing overlapping, and a screening question needs no escape option.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'talk with hearing people every week' word for word, and nothing about a product or the founder's own terms reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with an obvious yes-or-no answer, though the spoken form leaves off the closing 'Yes or no.' that the screener template calls for.

screens.why1: After the screener about talking with hearing people every week, it makes sense to show me the idea before asking what I think of it, though going straight to it with nothing about my own last conversation feels a little quick.
screens.why2: The words are plain to me, but "you wear your lightweight glasses" made me stop: I don't own special glasses, so does it mean my own glasses or theirs?
screens.why3: Following hearing people face to face and losing the thread when I look away to read is my everyday life, so I can picture this right away.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It is shown openly as an idea to imagine, and it talks about reading the words and keeping eye contact, which is how I'd put it myself, with nothing of the maker's own jargon slipping through.
screens.why6: It is four sentences with no symbols, but it says "lightweight glasses" and "live captions inside the lens" twice, so heard aloud the middle drags and the second sentence adds nothing.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that shows live captions inside the lens. When people near you talk, their words appear in the lens as they speak. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I talk with hearing people every week, asking how often those conversations go wrong is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Fell through" makes me think of a plan that got cancelled, not a conversation I couldn't follow, so I'd have to read it twice to guess what it means.
screens.why3: I talk with hearing people all month, so I'd be guessing a rough count, and I'd also be unsure which conversations count as having fallen through.
screens.why4: A number box, None, and I can't recall cover every answer I could give, and the label is clear.
screens.why5: "Fell through" drifts from what the trouble really is for me, losing track of what people are saying, and the card itself warns against that phrase.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, though "A number of conversations last month" sounds a little stiff when heard.
screens.why7: The box counts conversations a month, in the right unit, but the verb is the vague "fell through" that the card says to avoid, so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many conversations with hearing people could you not follow? [ box ] conversations last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: Asking what the glasses would be worth makes sense right after I've seen the AirCaps card, but it sits under 'What you do today' and comes straight after a question about conversations falling through, so it lands a bit abruptly.
screens.why2: 'Worth to you up front' and 'a month' are how I already think about hearing aids and caption apps, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I've paid for hearing aids and caption subscriptions out of my own pocket, so I know what I'd put down for glasses and what I'd stand each month.
screens.why4: Both ladders are complete and don't overlap, $599 is an odd figure but plainly a real sticker price, and 'I wouldn't pay for this' and 'I can't say' both fit.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's own name AirCaps reaches me, which is shown on purpose, and nothing else of the company's plan or its terms for people like me leaks in.
screens.why6: Each step reads four short options and then two, with one 'Or say: I can't say', so I could hold it hearing it once (or reading it on screen, as I would).
screens.why7: Both ladders are on the money measure with an edge exactly at the founder's $599 and $20, two bands below and three from it plus 'I wouldn't pay' against, and the one escape 'I can't say' sits apart, so the belief can be supported or refuted.
screens.instead: Under 'What it would be worth' rather than 'What you do today': What would AirCaps be worth to you up front? Under $250 · $250 to under $599 · $599 to under $1,000 · $1,000 to under $2,500 · $2,500 or more · I wouldn't pay for this · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after I gave a price, asking what would make it worth more is the natural next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: It reads my own answer back as I'd say it, about $250 to $600 up front, and the question is short and plain.
screens.why3: I know what I'd want from captions: keeping up at a noisy dinner table or a fast meeting, so I can answer from my own week.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: AirCaps was named on the idea card I was shown on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms comes through.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is one short question with a dollar range that says easily, and nothing for the eye only.

screens.why1: Right after I've put a price on AirCaps, it makes sense to ask whether I'd be the one deciding or whether my partner, my insurance or my employer would come into it.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself; I'd read 'something like this' as hearing aids or a captioning app, which I have actually bought.
screens.why3: I know who signed off on my last hearing aids and captioning apps; sometimes it was just me, and sometimes insurance or a vocational rehab counsellor had the say.
screens.why4: The four cover me alone, my spouse, several people (insurance plus audiologist), and someone else paying, such as an employer accommodation or VR; 'I can't say' covers never having bought one.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's pitch or roles reaches me; it only says 'anyone else'.
screens.why6: Heard once, 'someone else had to agree; several people had to agree; it was someone else's call' blur together, and a yes-or-no stem followed by four non-yes-no options takes a second to switch gears.
screens.why7: Nobody else tested on the payer's past form: 'anyone else' in the stem, the four fixed answers in order from alone to someone else's call, one for and three against, and 'I can't say' apart.
screens.instead: The last time you bought something for your hearing, like hearing aids or a captioning app, who decided? I decided on my own · Someone else had to agree · Several people had to agree · It was someone else's call · I can't say

screens.why1: After the idea card, the price and who else has to agree, asking whether I'd actually order a pair is the natural last question, though the 'What you do today' kicker doesn't really fit a would-you question.
screens.why2: 'Caption glasses' and 'free returns' are words I'd use myself, and I'd understand it the first time I read or heard it.
screens.why3: Whether I'd order glasses I could send back is my own call, from my own hearing and the money I have, so I can answer it straight off.
screens.why4: The four options cover firm and soft yes and no, but 'after trying a pair first' sits close to ordering with free returns, which is already a way of trying a pair, so I'd wonder where I'd even try them first.
screens.why5: It is the founder's step whole, with free returns and the glasses named, and nothing beyond the idea card I was shown reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one question and four options I can hold, but the first two options are long and repeat 'caption glasses', so the first one is a mouthful heard aloud.
screens.why7: The measure, the order, the firm-and-soft balance and the missing escape all meet the card, and the first option is the step as asked, but the soft yes's smaller step only barely differs from free returns, so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you order the caption glasses with free returns, or not? Yes, I'd order the caption glasses with free returns · Probably, after trying a pair in a shop first · Probably not · No
